newsitem.title: FRANCE: Small German rate rise could be positive - Delors.
newsitem.headline: Small German rate rise could be positive - Delors.

text.p: A small increase in German interest rates could be positive if it helped prop up Europe's currencies ahead of the launch of a single European currency, former European Commission president Jacques Delors wrote in French magazine Nouvel Observateur.

While even a very small increase would be not be a good thing psychologically for German and European business "it would on the other hand be positive to not have an excessive weakening of European currencies on the eve of the final decisions about the launch of the euro," he said.

While financial markets would ultimately determine the exchange rate between the euro and the dollar, it was nevertheless "not without importance that the mark showed a certain firmness against the U.S. currency in the coming months, supporting other European currencies in turn".
Delors said that for Europe to have an influence the euro must become a reserve currency for central banks throughout the world, attract savings and become major currency for trade.
"Everyone must wish for the birth of a stable euro, neither too strong not too weak," Delors said.

He also said if the U.S. Federal Reserve were to raise U.S. interest rates again the German Bundesbank would have no choice but to follow to prevent another rally in the dollar, which is trading at a near eight-year high against the mark.

Delors said the mark's weakness could be explained partly by financial markets' view that a large number of countries would take part in a single currency from the outset but also by Germany's internal problems.

"It is true that internal reasons also explain the current weakness of the German currency: an economy that can't find its way back to relatively strong growth, the massive unemployment, a political crisis which is blocking important fiscal reform aimed...at reviving the German economic machine," Delors said.
